interactions.summary: Jiang doubles down that free will is God's unconditional love, narrows the parent analogy by admitting the universe still has limits, and then fields a question about whether Eden undercuts human freedom.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Jiang-led classroom exchange with student objections and follow-up question

claims.claim: Jiang states the packet's strongest theological thesis: because God is perfect creator and loves creation, he gives freedom to the universe, and free will is the ultimate law through which divine love is expressed.
In the same move, Jiang insists that God does not command good, evil, or imitation of himself; divine love is noncoercive rather than instructional.
A student objects that parental love cannot simply mean unconditional permission, because being a parent also includes responsibility and correction.
Another student sharpens the same objection by distinguishing moral support from unrestricted permission, noting that free will cannot mean parents let a child do anything at all.
Jiang partially concedes that point by saying the universe has rules and limits, so free will operates inside boundaries rather than as absolute power.

A student then asks whether Eden complicates the whole framework, since Adam and Eve may not have understood good and evil before the tree and thus may not have possessed full free will in the first place.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang turns free will from one doctrine among others into the supreme law of reality because it is how God loves creation.
signature_moments.source_phrase: Free will is the ultimate law of the universe
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is a core Jiang compression of Dante's cosmology into an existential claim about love, law, and human freedom.

signature_moments.moment: Divine love is defined negatively as a love that never orders you toward either good or evil.
signature_moments.source_phrase: God will not ask you to do good. God will not ask you to do evil
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It radicalizes the noncoercive model and explains why Jiang keeps resisting judge and experiment metaphors.

signature_moments.moment: The class immediately stress-tests Jiang's analogy by forcing a distinction between bounded freedom and absolute permission, then carries that tension back into Eden itself.
signature_moments.source_phrase: there are rules to the universe
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This shows the classroom not merely receiving doctrine but using objections to expose the hardest unresolved edge in the free-will model.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Jiang's phrase for free will as the deepest structure of reality because it is the form divine love takes.
Expanded here into a noncoercive theology in which God supports rather than compels the human creature.

glossary_terms.term: tree of the knowledge of good and evil
glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Introduced as the Edenic problem that may complicate whether humans possessed meaningful free choice before the fall.

chronology_notes.note: This packet stays within the June 15 classroom sequence and sets up a move into Eden interpretation, but it does not by itself establish a dated shift across sources.
